raw_response:
Thinking through this as the farmer, then laying out the full plan.

---

I've been working this land for 25 years, so I know what to expect. My 65 mu keeps me busy — wheat and maize are the backbone, about 40 mu in that double-crop rotation, and the rest I split between stevia, watermelon, chili, and cabbage. Stevia has been good money the last few years, so I keep 8 mu in it. Watermelon is higher risk but the returns are worth it if the summer goes well.

For wheat, I always put down a compound fertilizer base before planting — maybe 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu — and then I topdress urea at jointing if the leaves look a bit pale. The extension station has been saying to cut back on nitrogen, but I've seen what happens when I apply too little: the yield drops and I lose more money than I saved on fertilizer. So I keep N around 18 kg per mu total. I do 3 irrigations for wheat: winter water before freeze-up, another at jointing, one at heading. Sometimes a fourth if it's dry at grain filling, but that costs money.

Right after wheat harvest — early June, no time to waste — I plant hybrid maize. I stopped deep plowing between crops a few years ago because there's just no time. I use a rotary mulcher or sometimes just plant directly into the stubble if I can get a no-till seeder. For maize I cut back a little on water — usually 1 or 2 irrigations unless it's a dry summer. Maize doesn't need as much watching.

The other crops take more labor. Stevia especially — the leaf harvest in summer is very demanding, my wife and I can't do it alone, I hire 3 or 4 workers for about 20 days. Watermelon needs careful irrigation timing and I have to watch for disease. Chili and cabbage are smaller plots, more for income diversification. Cabbage I plant in late July for autumn harvest — it fits nicely after some of the spring crops come off.

The tight spot every year is the June window between wheat harvest and maize planting. Everything has to happen in about 5 days. I've learned to have the maize seed, fertilizer, and a machinery operator lined up a week before wheat harvest.
